extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, math journal editors, academic publishers, and members of mathematical societies (e.g., AMS Council)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance, critique, and concrete suggestions for how mathematics journals (and mathematical societies) should operate: editorial practice, peer review purpose, awards, acceptance rates, electronic publishing, and community relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors' Suggestions as recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: A small number of articles the editors choose to highlight (Editors’ Suggestions) which are viewed as a minor research award and can be listed on authors' CVs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlighting selected papers formally and on the website provides visible recognition; such selections function as minor awards that help authors' careers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outstanding referee award to encourage quick and thorough refereeing
rubrics_metrics.description: An award (e.g., APS Outstanding Referee) instituted to encourage quick and thorough refereeing; lifetime award with a diploma/plaque and taken seriously via nominations by Associate Editors and editorial discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguished-referee awards validate otherwise-anonymous referee work, provide community recognition useful for departmental/administrative review, and should be selected through a serious nomination/discussion process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community-friendly editorial behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should operate in a way that 'validates the significance of papers needed for job related purposes, helps the authors to improve the style, does not bite newcomers, and does not second guess their experimental finding.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should provide constructive feedback, quick turnaround, and an overall supportive relationship with their research community rather than being needlessly hostile or obstructive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review as certificate of validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review should provide a certificate that someone anonymous read the paper and takes responsibility for its validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The function of peer review includes checking correctness and producing an accountable stamp of validity — journals should ensure this role is actually fulfilled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal validation via journal reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals provide formal validation (something to list on CVs) and different journals carry different prestige levels affecting jobs, promotions, and grants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintaining and communicating clear standards of prestige and quality helps employers and committees evaluate candidates; journals should be conscious of their role in career signaling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate technical validity checking from evaluative selection
rubrics_metrics.description: The peer-review/certification aspect (validity) should be separated from the evaluation aspect (novelty/importance) which requires competition between journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider models where a correctness-checking venue (mega journal) certifies papers for correctness while other venues compete to label and highlight important or novel work, reducing multiple submissions and ethical costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent, timely editorial decisions and mandatory referee reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial decisions should be transparent and timely; the practice of returning papers after long delays without any referee report is unacceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals must ensure referees provide substantive reports and editors make decisions within reasonable timeframes; avoid arbitrary rejections after long waits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mega journal model: accept based on correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed 'mega journal' (or several 'baby megas') that accepts papers based on correctness only, with authors optionally forwarding arXiv postings; editors divided by arXiv subject areas, initial screening to send ~30–40% for review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This model focuses on verifying proofs and correctness rather than novelty, allows broad accessibility, and supports selection and prestige via separate mechanisms (awards or bids).

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow multiple selection mechanisms (awards/overlay/journal bids)
rubrics_metrics.description: General/top journals or specialized journals could place bids or make independent selections for the best papers; overlay journals could link to arXiv versions; papers could receive multiple awards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decoupling publication from selection allows authors choice and multiple recognitions, reducing pressure to target a single high-prestige venue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt competitive conference-style selection where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce a competitive conference system (as in CS theory) requiring prior arXiv posting and keeping track of 'verified' papers accepted to the correctness-checking venue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conference-style review could speed dissemination and foster progress on emerging tools/ideas; it can help level the playing field for underfunded researchers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase acceptance rates for public-society journals
rubrics_metrics.description: Public-society journals (e.g., AMS journals) should consider higher acceptance rates and act as large, free, friendly but thorough publication venues for papers that don't meet top-tier thresholds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher acceptance can serve a public-good role, reduce gatekeeping, and provide reliable outlets for legitimate work that would otherwise be marginalized by low-acceptance elite journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity as a desirable feature
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians should value brevity: many papers are longer than needed and brevity is a feature not a bug.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and authors should encourage concise presentations; longer papers are sometimes necessary but unnecessary length consumes resources and slows refereeing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Move fully to electronic publishing and remove print-driven limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Stop wasting paper and fully move to electronic publishing; do not limit numbers of papers or pages — aim for as many good papers as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Digital publishing removes physical constraints; journals should eliminate artificial page limits and embrace scalability, focusing on quality rather than arbitrary quotas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve electronic editorial systems and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Improve editorial systems to be more transparent and electronically robust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Better workflows, visible status updates, and clearer handling of submissions/referees will reduce delays and frustrations; publish clear criteria and timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensate and professionalize editorial work
rubrics_metrics.description: Help editors work as a team and incentivize them financially (e.g., pay for 20% employment to experts worldwide to help run the journal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional support for editors reduces burnout, speeds processing, and improves consistency; societies should invest in part-time paid staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create specialized outlets for surveys
rubrics_metrics.description: Set up new math journals fully dedicated to survey articles, both solicited and contributed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey journals serve different community needs and provide venues for synthesis and exposition distinct from original-research journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create appeals procedures and new senior-editor roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish an appeals procedure and add a new type of senior editors who take appeals and editorial quality seriously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A formal appeals mechanism increases fairness and accountability; senior editors should review contested decisions to ensure consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institute multiple awards within journals
rubrics_metrics.description: Institute awards for best long, short, and survey articles in the journal and for best referees; make an effort to be fair by taking input from all editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal awards promote recognition, incentivize quality submissions and refereeing, and provide alternative signals of excellence beyond journal prestige.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularly study journal practices and appoint oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Societies should conduct journal studies, appoint roles like a 'Chair of journal innovation,' and engage with resources (e.g., Journalology) to learn from other publishers' studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ongoing empirical study and dedicated oversight will help societies modernize practices and adopt evidence-based reforms rather than ad-hoc changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid editorial conflict of interest between helping authors and preserving exclusivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors' incentives can conflict: helping authors might hurt the journal (by making mediocre work acceptable) and vice versa; this conflict reduces assistance to authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial structures should minimize perverse incentives so editors can assist authors in improving correctness without fearing loss of journal selectivity; separating correctness certification from prestige selection is one remedy.
